title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt X: The Watch in the Hall (lines 662–709)
part: Fitt X · The Watch in the Hall (lines 662–709)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 25–27, lines 662–709 (fitt X). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Ðā him Hrōþgār gewāt mid his hæleþa gedryht,
eodur Scyldinga ūt of healle;
sentences.l: Then for himself Hrothgar went, with his company of heroes, the fence of the Scyldings, out of the hall;
sentences.i: Then Hrothgar went out of the hall with his company of warriors, the shield of the Scyldings;
sentences.n: The sentence opens a new scene, so Klaeber starts a new paragraph. ‘Ðā him Hrōþgār gewāt’ is ‘then Hrothgar went’: ‘gewāt’ is the past of ‘gewītan’, ‘depart’, and ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, ‘for himself’, which Old English often adds to verbs of going and which English drops; I keep it in the literal line. ‘mid his hæleþa gedryht’ is ‘with his company of heroes’: ‘gedryht’ is a feminine noun, ‘company’, in the dative after ‘mid’, and ‘hæleþa’ is a genitive plural. ‘eodur Scyldinga’ is in apposition to Hrothgar: ‘eodor’ is an ‘enclosure, fence’ and so a protector (the same word was rendered ‘fence of the Scyldings’ at 428), and ‘Scyldinga’ is a genitive plural. The name is spelled with ‘þ’ here, ‘Hrōþgār’, and with ‘ð’ elsewhere; both are the same name.

sentences.t:
wolde wīgfruma Wealhþēo sēcan,
cwēn tō gebeddan.
sentences.l: The war-chief wished to seek Wealhtheow, the queen, as bedfellow.
sentences.i: The war-chief meant to go to Wealhtheow, the queen, to share her bed.
sentences.n: ‘wolde’ is the past of ‘willan’, ‘wish, intend’, with the infinitive ‘sēcan’, ‘seek, go to’. ‘wīgfruma’ is the subject, a compound of ‘wīg’, ‘war’, and ‘fruma’, ‘beginning, first one, leader’, so ‘war-chief’, still Hrothgar. ‘Wealhþēo’ is the queen’s name, the object of ‘sēcan’; at 612 in fitt IX it was spelled ‘Wealhþēow’, and the final ‘w’ is simply missing here. ‘cwēn’ is in apposition. ‘tō gebeddan’ is ‘as bedfellow’: ‘gebedda’ is a weak noun, ‘bed-companion’, and ‘gebeddan’ is a dative with ‘tō’, ‘for a bedfellow’, that is, as his wife. The king leaves the hall to sleep: at 646 in fitt IX he wished to seek ‘ǣfenræste’, ‘evening-rest’, and this is that going.

sentences.l: Had the King-glory, against Grendel, as men heard tell, set a hall-guard;
sentences.i: The King of glory had set a hall-guard against Grendel, as men have heard;
sentences.n: The verb comes first, ‘Hæfde … āseted’, ‘had set’, a perfect made from ‘habban’ and the past participle of ‘āsettan’, ‘set, appoint’, which Old English puts at the end of the clause. ‘Kyningwuldor’ is a name of God, and the packet’s apparatus shows editors taking it apart: Kemble (with a query), Thorpe and Sedgefield read two words, ‘kyning[a] wuldor’, ‘glory of kings’, while Klaeber prints one compound, which I take as ‘King of glory’ (‘wuldor’ is ‘glory’), literal ‘King-glory’. Either way it is the Lord, who is said to have set the guard. ‘Grendle tōgēanes’ is ‘against Grendel’: ‘tōgēanes’ governs the dative. ‘swā guman gefrungon’ is ‘as men heard tell’, the house rendering of ‘gefrignan’ (literally ‘learn by asking’; it is the verb of ‘gefrægn’ in the poem’s formulas), here a past plural, a parenthesis that vouches for the report. ‘seleweard’ is ‘hall-guard’ (‘sele’, ‘hall’, and ‘weard’, ‘guard’), and the next lines show that the guard is Beowulf.

sentences.t:
sundọrnytte behēold
ymb aldor Dena, eotonweard’ ābēad.
sentences.l: special service he performed about the chief of the Danes, a giant-guard he offered.
sentences.i: He did a special service for the lord of the Danes: he offered himself as a guard against the giant.
sentences.n: The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘sundọrnytte’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; it is the first one in this part, and ‘trūwọde’ at 669 has another. ‘sundornytt’ is a compound of ‘sundor’, ‘apart, special’, and ‘nytt’, ‘use, service’, so ‘special service’; it is the accusative object of ‘behēold’, the past of ‘behealdan’, ‘hold, keep, carry out’. ‘ymb aldor Dena’ is ‘about the chief of the Danes’: ‘ymb’ takes the accusative, ‘aldor’ is ‘lord, chief’ (Hrothgar), and ‘Dena’ is a genitive plural. The end of the unit is uncertain. ‘eotonweard’’ carries Klaeber’s apostrophe, which marks a lost final letter, most likely the ‘e’ of ‘eotonwearde’ dropped before the ‘ā’ of ‘ābēad’; if so, the full form ends in a dative ending (as in Binz’s ‘eotenwearde’), not the bare accusative my literal line makes of it, so the case is open as well as the sense. ‘eoton’ is ‘giant’ and ‘weard’ is ‘guard’, so ‘giant-guard’ is the thing offered, and ‘ābēad’ (past of ‘ābēodan’, ‘offer, announce’) would then mean that he offered or proclaimed himself a guard against the giant, which is Grendel. The apparatus shows editors disagreeing: Kemble reads ‘ēotnes weard ābād’, ‘the giant’s guard waited’, Binz ‘eotenwearde bēad’, ‘offered to the giant-guard’, and Sedgefield ‘eotonweard ābād’. My literal line follows Klaeber, and the idiomatic line gives the sense I think he intends; the grammar of the last half-line is a guess.

sentences.t:
Hūru Gēata lēod georne trūwọde
mōdgan mægnes, Metodes hyldo. —
sentences.l: Indeed the Geats’ man eagerly trusted in his proud strength, in the Measurer’s favor. —
sentences.i: Indeed the man of the Geats trusted firmly in his own proud strength and in the favor of the Lord. —
sentences.n: ‘Hūru’ is ‘indeed, at least’. ‘Gēata lēod’ is ‘man of the Geats’ (Beowulf): ‘lēod’ is the masculine singular ‘man’, as in ‘Gēata lēod’ at 625, not the plural ‘lēode’, ‘people’. ‘georne’ is the adverb ‘eagerly, firmly’. ‘trūwode’ is the past of ‘trūwian’, ‘trust’, which takes a genitive, and the dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘trūwọde’ is the same metrical sign as at 667. The apparatus lists Sievers, Holthausen and Schücking as reading ‘trēowde’, a shorter form with one syllable fewer, which is what the dot seems to point to: the vowel is written but not counted. ‘mōdgan mægnes’ is a genitive, ‘of proud-minded strength’, the case ‘trūwian’ takes here. ‘Metodes hyldo’ is ‘the Measurer’s favor’, a second object, but ‘hyldo’ is the nominative or accusative form of the feminine ‘hyldu’, ‘favor, grace’ (a genitive would be ‘hylde’), so it does not match ‘mægnes’; I take it as an accusative, and the construction is irregular, so that is a guess. ‘Metod’, ‘the Measurer’, is the house rendering for God as the one who metes out fates; the idiomatic line says ‘the Lord’. The dash is Klaeber’s and marks a break before the arming scene is described.

sentences.t:
Ðā hē him of dyde īsernbyrnan,
helm of hafelan, sealde his hyrsted sweord,
īrena cyst ombihtþegne,
ond gehealdan hēt hildegeatwe.
sentences.l: Then he from himself took the iron-mail, the helmet from his head, gave his adorned sword, the choicest of irons, to the attendant, and bade him keep the battle-gear.
sentences.i: Then he took off his iron mail-shirt and the helmet from his head, and gave his ornamented sword, the choicest of blades, to his attendant, and told him to keep the war-gear safe.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā hē him of dyde’ is ‘then he took off from himself’: ‘of dyde’ is the past of ‘of dōn’, ‘take off’, and ‘him’ is again a reflexive dative. ‘īsernbyrnan’ is ‘iron mail-coat’, an accusative (weak plural or singular; the packet’s form does not tell me which, and I give the singular), and ‘helm of hafelan’ is ‘helmet from his head’. ‘sealde his hyrsted sweord’ is ‘gave his adorned sword’: ‘hyrsted’ is the participle of ‘hyrstan’, ‘adorn’, and I take it as an adjective ‘ornamented’. ‘īrena cyst’ is ‘the choicest of irons’: ‘īren’ is both ‘iron’ and ‘sword’, ‘īrena’ is a genitive plural, and ‘cyst’ is ‘the choice, the best’. Klaeber prints ‘īrena’; the apparatus lists Sievers, Trautmann, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield as reading ‘īren[n]a’, with a doubled ‘n’, which is the same genitive plural spelled with its full ending, so the sense does not change. ‘ombihtþegne’ is the dative of ‘ombihtþegn’, ‘attendant, retainer’ (‘ombiht’ is ‘service, office’), the man who receives the gear. ‘ond gehealdan hēt’ is ‘and bade keep’: ‘hēt’ takes an infinitive, ‘gehealdan’, and the object is ‘hildegeatwe’, ‘battle-gear’ (an accusative plural). Beowulf will fight Grendel without sword or mail.

sentences.t:
Gespræc þā se gōda gylpworda sum,
Bēowulf Gēata, ǣr hē on bed stige:
sentences.l: Spoke then the good one a certain one of boast-words, Beowulf of the Geats, before he onto bed climbed:
sentences.i: Then the good man, Beowulf of the Geats, made one of his boasts before he climbed into bed:
sentences.n: ‘Gespræc’ is the past of ‘gesprecan’, ‘speak, say’. ‘se gōda’ is ‘the good one’, a weak adjective used as a noun, and the name follows in apposition: ‘Bēowulf Gēata’, ‘Beowulf of the Geats’. ‘gylpworda sum’ is ‘a certain one of boast-words’: ‘sum’ means ‘one, a certain’ and takes a genitive plural, ‘gylpworda’, so it comes to ‘one of his boasts’, a boast among others. ‘ǣr hē on bed stige’ is ‘before he climbed onto the bed’; ‘stige’ is a subjunctive of ‘stīgan’, ‘climb’ (Klaeber prints no macron, which fits the past subjunctive), the mood ‘ǣr’ takes when the event is still ahead. The colon is Klaeber’s and the speech follows.

sentences.t:
‘Nō ic mē an herewæsmun hnāgran talige
gūþgeweorca, þonne Grendel hine;
sentences.l: ‘Not I myself in war-strength lower reckon, in battle-works, than Grendel (reckons) himself;
sentences.i: ‘I do not count myself lower in strength for war or in deeds of battle than Grendel counts himself;
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark begins Beowulf’s speech. ‘Nō ic mē … talige’ is ‘I do not reckon myself’: ‘talige’ is the first person singular of ‘talian’, ‘reckon, count’, and ‘mē’ is a reflexive dative. ‘hnāgran’ is the comparative of ‘hnāh’, ‘low, mean’, here ‘lower’ in worth. ‘an herewæsmun’ is ‘in war-strength’: ‘an’ is a spelling of ‘on’, and ‘herewæsmun’ is a dative plural of a compound of ‘here’, ‘army’, and ‘wæstm’, ‘growth, strength’, a word I know only from this line, so ‘war-strength’ is a guess. The apparatus lists other readings, ‘-wæs[t]mum’ (Grundtvig, adding a ‘t’), ‘-wǣsum’ and ‘-wǣpnum’, ‘war-weapons’ (Trautmann), and Klaeber prints ‘herewæsmun’. ‘gūþgeweorca’ is a genitive plural of respect, ‘in battle-works’. ‘þonne Grendel hine’ is ‘than Grendel (reckons) himself’: ‘hine’ is the accusative object of an understood ‘talað’, ‘reckons’, so Beowulf measures himself against Grendel’s own opinion of himself; ‘hine’ is not an emphatic ‘himself’ added to Grendel.

sentences.t:
forþan ic hine sweorde swebban nelle,
aldre benēotan, þēah ic eal mæge;
sentences.l: therefore I him with sword put-to-sleep will not, of life deprive, though I all can;
sentences.i: so I will not kill him with a sword and rob him of his life, though I am well able;
sentences.n: ‘forþan’ is ‘therefore’. ‘swebban’ is ‘put to sleep’, the old word for ‘kill’ (as ‘āswefede’ in the part before). ‘nelle’ is ‘ne wille’, ‘will not’, so ‘hine … swebban nelle’ is ‘I will not kill him’. ‘sweorde’ is a dative of the instrument, ‘with a sword’. ‘aldre benēotan’ is ‘deprive of life’: ‘benēotan’ is ‘rob of’, and it takes the dative of the thing taken, ‘aldre’, ‘life’. ‘þēah ic eal mæge’ is ‘though I can do it all’, with ‘eal’ either the object of ‘mæge’ (‘all’) or an adverb (‘wholly’), the sense being the same, and ‘mæge’ a present subjunctive of ‘magan’, ‘be able’. Beowulf means that he is able but will not use a sword.

sentences.l: he knows not of those good things, that he strike against me, hew the shield, though he be bold in hate-works;
sentences.i: he has no knowledge of the good art of striking back at me and hewing my shield to pieces, brave though he is in deeds of malice;
sentences.n: ‘nāt’ is ‘ne wāt’, ‘does not know’, with a genitive, ‘þāra gōda’, ‘of those good things’. The sense of this phrase is a guess: I take ‘gōda’ as a noun, ‘good things, skills’, and the next clause says which skills. The apparatus shows Thorpe reading ‘þǣre gūðe’, ‘of that war’, so the sense may be ‘the arts of that fighting’. ‘þæt hē mē ongēan sleâ’ is ‘that he strike against me’: ‘sleâ’ is a present subjunctive of ‘slēan’, ‘strike’, and the circumflex is Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel. ‘rand gehēawe’ is ‘hew the shield’, with ‘gehēawe’ a second subjunctive and ‘rand’ its accusative object. ‘þēah ðe hē rōf siê’ is ‘though he be bold’: ‘siê’ is a subjunctive of ‘wesan’, ‘be’, with a circumflex for the same reason, and ‘rōf’ takes the genitive ‘nīþgeweorca’, ‘in hate-works’, hostile deeds. Grendel has no weapons, so he does not know how to fight with them.

sentences.t:
ac wit on niht sculon
secge ofersittan, gif hē gesēcean dear
wīg ofer wǣpen, ond siþðan wītig God
on swā hwæþere hond hālig Dryhten
mǣrðo dēme, swā him gemet þince.’
sentences.l: but we two by night shall forgo the sword, if he dare seek battle without weapon, and afterwards wise God, the holy Lord, on whichever hand may assign glories, as to him may seem fitting.’
sentences.i: but we two shall do without the sword tonight, if he dares to seek battle without a weapon, and afterwards may the wise God, the holy Lord, award the glory to whichever side, as seems fitting to him.’
sentences.n: ‘wit’ is the dual pronoun, ‘we two’, Beowulf and Grendel, with ‘sculon’ as ‘shall’. ‘secge ofersittan’ is ‘forgo the sword’: ‘ofersittan’ is ‘sit over, hold back from’, and I take ‘secge’ as a dative of ‘secg’, ‘sword’. There are two words ‘secg’, the masculine ‘man’ (as in ‘mīnra secga’ at 633) and ‘sword’, and both have the dative ‘secge’, so the form does not decide. To ‘sit over’ a man would have to mean ‘overcome’ him, which does not suit a promise to fight without weapons, so ‘sword’ is a guess from the sense of the sentence. The manuscript has ‘het’ for ‘hē’ in ‘gif hē gesēcean dear’, as the apparatus says, and Kemble corrected it; Klaeber prints ‘hē’ and marks the ‘ē’ in italic. ‘dear’ is the present of ‘durran’, ‘dare’, with ‘gesēcean’, ‘seek out’, and ‘wīg ofer wǣpen’ is ‘battle without weapon’, ‘ofer’ here being ‘beyond, without’, which is how I take it. Then a second clause: ‘ond siþðan wītig God … hālig Dryhten mǣrðo dēme’ is ‘and afterwards may wise God, holy Lord, assign glories’, with a subjunctive ‘dēme’ of ‘dēman’, ‘judge, decree’, and ‘mǣrðo’ an accusative plural, ‘glories, honors’. ‘wītig’ is ‘wise, knowing’. ‘on swā hwæþere hond’ is ‘on whichever hand’, that is, to whichever side: ‘swā hwæþer’ is ‘whichever of two’, and ‘hwæþere’ is the feminine accusative agreeing with ‘hond’ after ‘on’ of direction. ‘swā him gemet þince’ is ‘as to him may seem fitting’, a subjunctive of ‘þyncan’. ‘Dryhten’ is ‘Lord’, as in the earlier parts. The closing quotation mark ends the speech begun at 677.

sentences.t:
Hylde hine þā heaþodēor, hlēorbolster onfēng
eorles andwlitan, ond hine ymb monig
snellīc sǣrinc selereste gebēah.
sentences.l: Bowed himself then the battle-bold one, the cheek-pillow received the earl’s face, and around him many a bold sea-warrior onto hall-rest bowed.
sentences.i: Then the battle-bold man lay down, and the pillow took the earl’s face, and around him many a bold seafarer bent himself to his bed in the hall.
sentences.n: A new paragraph after the speech. ‘Hylde hine’ is ‘inclined himself’, the past of ‘hyldan’, ‘lean, bow’, with a reflexive accusative: he lay down. ‘heaþodēor’ is ‘battle-bold’ (‘heaþo’, ‘battle’, and ‘dēor’, ‘bold’), Beowulf. ‘hlēorbolster’ is ‘cheek-pillow’, the subject of ‘onfēng’, ‘received’, and ‘eorles andwlitan’ is ‘the earl’s face’, the object. The apparatus says that Kemble and Thorpe print it as two words, ‘hlēor bolster’. ‘ond hine ymb monig snellīc sǣrinc’ is ‘and around him many a bold sea-warrior’ (‘snellīc’ is ‘bold, quick’, ‘sǣrinc’ is a compound of ‘sǣ’, ‘sea’, and ‘rinc’, ‘warrior’, so one of the Geats), and the verb is at the end, ‘gebēah’, the past of ‘gebūgan’, ‘bow, bend’, with ‘selereste’ a feminine singular whose dative and accusative forms coincide, taken here as ‘to hall-rest’, that is to his bed in the hall. ‘hine ymb’ is ‘around him’, with ‘ymb’ standing after its pronoun, and the verb ‘gebēah’ comes at the end of the clause.

sentences.l: None of them thought that he thence should ever again seek home-love, his folk or noble city, where he was brought up;
sentences.i: Not one of them thought that he would ever again leave the hall to seek his beloved homeland, his people or the noble town where he was raised;
sentences.n: ‘Nǣnig heora þōhte’ is ‘none of them thought’: ‘þōhte’ is the past of ‘þencan’, ‘think’, and ‘heora’ a genitive plural. The ‘þæt’ clause says what none of them thought: ‘þæt hē þanon scolde eft … gesēcean’, ‘that he should from there again seek’; ‘scolde’ is ‘was to’; as the content of a thought it reads ‘would’, though the form does not show the mood. ‘eardlufan’ is the accusative of ‘eardlufu’, ‘home-love’, a beloved dwelling or homeland, and ‘folc oþðe frēoburh’ stands in apposition: ‘his people or his noble town’, ‘frēoburh’ being ‘free-borough’, a noble stronghold. ‘þǣr hē āfēded wæs’ is ‘where he was raised’, the participle of ‘āfēdan’, ‘nourish, bring up’. The point is that the Geats thought Beowulf would die.

sentences.t:
ac hīe hæfdon gefrūnen, þæt hīe ǣr tō fela micles
in þǣm wīnsele wældēað fornam,
Denigea lēode.
sentences.l: but they had heard tell, that them earlier far too many in that wine-hall slaughter-death had taken off, the Danes’ people.
sentences.i: but they had heard that death in battle had already carried off far too many of the Danish people in that wine-hall.
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’, and it introduces what the Geats knew instead. ‘hīe hæfdon gefrūnen’ is ‘they had heard tell’, the perfect of ‘gefrignan’ (the participle ‘gefrūnen’). Inside the ‘þæt’ clause ‘hīe’ is ‘them’, the Danes, so the same word means two different groups in one sentence, which is how Old English reads. ‘ǣr’ is ‘earlier’, ‘tō fela micles’ is ‘far too many’ (‘tō fela’ is ‘too many’ and ‘micles’ a genitive of degree, ‘by much’), ‘in þǣm wīnsele’ is ‘in that wine-hall’, ‘wældēað’ is ‘slaughter-death’, the subject, and ‘fornam’ is the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take off, destroy’. ‘Denigea lēode’ is ‘the Danes’ people’ in apposition to ‘hīe’, with ‘lēode’ an accusative plural of ‘lēod’, ‘people’. The apparatus shows scholars unhappy with ‘hīe ǣr’: Thorpe reads ‘hyra’ (with a query), Grein and Grundtvig ‘þætte ǣr’, Bugge ‘þæt ǣr’, Kluge and Sedgefield ‘hiera’. The sense is much the same in each.

sentences.t:
Ac him Dryhten forgeaf
wīgspēda gewiofu, Wedera leōdum,
frōfor ond fultum, þæt hīe fēond heora
ðurh ānes cræft ealle ofercōmon,
selfes mihtum.
sentences.l: But to them the Lord gave the webs of war-successes, to the Weders’ people, comfort and help, so that they all overcame their foe through one man’s craft, by his own might.
sentences.i: But the Lord granted the Weders the weaving of success in war, comfort and aid, so that through the strength of one man they all overcame their enemy, by his own might.
sentences.n: ‘Ac him Dryhten forgeaf’ is ‘but to them the Lord gave’, with ‘him’ the Geats, and ‘Wedera leōdum’ a dative plural in apposition, ‘to the people of the Weders’ (‘Wedera’ and ‘Gēata’ name the same people). ‘wīgspēda gewiofu’ is ‘the webs of war-successes’: ‘spēd’ is ‘success, speed’ and ‘gewiofu’ is a neuter plural, ‘woven things, webs’, a picture of fate as weaving that I take literally in the first line; ‘weaving of success’ in the second. ‘frōfor ond fultum’ is ‘comfort and help’, accusatives in apposition. ‘þæt hīe fēond heora … ofercōmon’ is a result clause, ‘so that they overcame their foe’: ‘ofercōmon’ is the past plural of ‘ofercuman’, ‘overcome’, with ‘fēond’ the same in the singular and the plural and ‘ealle’ ‘all’, which could go with ‘hīe’ or with ‘fēond’; I take ‘they all’ and a single foe. ‘ðurh ānes cræft’ is ‘through one man’s craft, strength’ (Beowulf’s), and ‘selfes mihtum’ is ‘by his own might’, ‘selfes’ a genitive of ‘self’ and ‘mihtum’ a dative plural. The sentence moves from the Geats’ doubt of their return to the poet’s assurance that God gave them victory.

sentences.t:
Sōð is gecȳþed,
þæt mihtig God manna cynnes
wēold wīdeferhð.
sentences.l: Truth is made known, that mighty God over mankind ruled for a wide lifetime.
sentences.i: It is a known truth that mighty God has ruled the race of men through all ages.
sentences.n: ‘Sōð is gecȳþed’ is ‘truth is made known’, the passive of ‘gecȳþan’. Klaeber has the poet speak here, not a character. ‘mihtig God … wēold’ is ‘mighty God ruled’, with ‘wēold’ the past of ‘wealdan’, which takes a genitive, ‘manna cynnes’, ‘of the kin of men’. The past tense gives a general truth, so the idiomatic line uses ‘has ruled’. ‘wīdeferhð’ is an adverb, ‘for a wide life’, meaning ‘for all time’; ‘ferhð’ is ‘life, spirit’. The apparatus reads ‘AB ride’; as I take it (the packet does not define the sigla), ‘A’ and ‘B’ are the two Thorkelin transcripts, which would give ‘ride’ where Klaeber prints ‘wīde’, and his italic ‘w’ marks that he changed the first letter; the apparatus also cites a ‘wīde-’ from Grundtvig’s translation. So the word is ‘wide’ with ‘ferhð’ in the sense of ‘life-time’, and the reading is partly a restoration.

sentences.t:
Cōm on wanre niht
scrīðan sceadugenga.
sentences.l: Came in the dark night gliding the shadow-walker.
sentences.i: In the dark night there came gliding the one who goes about in shadows.
sentences.n: ‘Cōm’ is the past of ‘cuman’, ‘come’, with the infinitive ‘scrīðan’, ‘glide’, as at 650. The subject follows the verbs, as is usual in a sentence of arrival: ‘sceadugenga’, a compound of ‘sceadu’, ‘shadow’, and ‘genga’, ‘goer’, so ‘shadow-walker’, which is Grendel (unnamed). ‘on wanre niht’ is ‘in the dark night’, a dative.

sentences.t:
Scēotend swǣfon,
þā þæt hornreced healdan scoldon,
ealle būton ānum.
sentences.l: The shooters slept, who the horn-hall should hold, all but one.
sentences.i: The warriors slept, those who were to guard the gabled hall, all but one.
sentences.n: ‘Scēotend’ is ‘shooters’, a plural noun from ‘scēotan’, ‘shoot’, used for warriors, and ‘swǣfon’ is the past plural of ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’. ‘þā … healdan scoldon’ is ‘who should hold’, with ‘þā’ a relative pronoun (it could also be ‘when’) and ‘scoldon’ a past plural. ‘hornreced’ is ‘horn-hall’, ‘reced’ being a ‘building, hall’, and ‘horn’ is probably the gable-ends, which curve like horns, but that is a guess. ‘ealle būton ānum’ is ‘all but one’, a dative after ‘būton’. The sleeping warriors are the Geats set to guard the hall, and the one awake is Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Þæt wæs yldum cūþ,
þæt hīe ne mōste, þā Metod nolde,
se s[c]ynscaþa under sceadu bregdan; —
sentences.l: That was to men known, that them not was-allowed, when the Measurer did not will it, the demon-scather under the shadows to drag; —
sentences.i: Men knew that, God being unwilling, the demon-foe was not allowed to drag them off under the shadows; —
sentences.n: ‘Þæt wæs yldum cūþ’ is ‘that was known to men’, with ‘yldum’ the dative plural of ‘ylde’, ‘men’, and the ‘þæt’ clause giving what was known. ‘þæt hīe ne mōste … bregdan’ is ‘that he might not drag them’: ‘mōste’ is the past of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’, ‘hīe’ is ‘them’, and ‘bregdan’ is ‘pull, drag, snatch’. ‘under sceadu’ is ‘under the shadows’, an accusative, and I cannot tell from the form whether one shadow or several is meant (‘the shadows’ is the English idiom), perhaps meaning down into the darkness of death. ‘þā Metod nolde’ is ‘when the Measurer was not willing’, with ‘nolde’ for ‘ne wolde’; ‘Metod’ is the house rendering for God. The subject is ‘se s[c]ynscaþa’, and the bracket is an emendation: the manuscript has ‘syn’, as the apparatus says, and Grein reads ‘s[c]in-’ or ‘s[c]yn-’, as Holthausen, Schücking and Chambers do. The packet’s apparatus sends the reader to Klaeber’s note on line 445 without giving it. I take ‘scynscaþa’ as ‘demon-foe’ or ‘phantom-scather’, from ‘scinn’, ‘phantom, evil spirit’, and ‘scaþa’, ‘harmer’ (the manuscript’s ‘synscaþa’ could be ‘sin-scather’ or an intensive ‘great harmer’, so my choice is a guess). The dash is Klaeber’s, and the sentence breaks off to turn back to Beowulf.

sentences.t:
ac hē wæccende wrāþum on andan
bād bolgenmōd beadwa geþinges.
sentences.l: but he, waking, in hostile anger awaited, swollen-minded, the outcome of battles.
sentences.i: But he stayed awake, swollen with wrath against his foe, and awaited the outcome of the fight.
sentences.n: ‘ac hē wæccende’ is ‘but he, awake’, with ‘wæccende’ the present participle of ‘wæccan’, ‘wake, watch’. ‘wrāþum on andan’ is ‘in hostile anger’: ‘anda’ is ‘anger, spite’, here a dative after ‘on’, and ‘wrāþum’ is a dative that can be read two ways: as an adjective agreeing with ‘andan’, ‘in hostile anger’, or as a noun, ‘toward the hostile one’. I take the phrase as anger against the foe, which is a guess about how the two words go together. ‘bād’ is the past of ‘bīdan’, ‘wait for’, which takes a genitive: ‘beadwa geþinges’, ‘the outcome of battles’. ‘geþinge’ is ‘agreement, issue, outcome’, the word behind ‘geþinged’ (‘appointed’) at 647; the apparatus has Kemble and Holthausen reading ‘beadwe’, a genitive singular, which would give ‘the outcome of the battle’. ‘bolgenmōd’ is ‘swollen-minded’, from ‘bolgen’, the participle of ‘belgan’, ‘swell with anger’, and ‘mōd’, ‘mind’.
